idiom_name: Ractor fan-out (or the Parallel/concurrent-ruby pools); threads only for I/O
implementation_notes: CRuby threads do not run Ruby code in parallel - the GVL serialises them - so the real substrate is Ractor: each Ractor holds its own GVL, cannot touch other Ractors' objects and exchanges shareable objects or messages, which maps cleanly onto independent subproblems (fork by creating a Ractor with a slice, join with take, combine the returned values). The ergonomic route for data-parallel leaves is a pool gem (Parallel over processes, or concurrent-ruby's executors). The classic thread-per-branch structure is not a parallel form on CRuby and should not be presented as one.
pitfalls: A Ractor block cannot close over outer locals: every input must be passed as an argument, and values crossing back must be shareable (a Proc or IO object raises).
Ractor creation is not free; keeping Ractor.new below the cut-off or inside deeply nested recursion multiplies overhead and can exhaust threads.
Exceptions inside a Ractor surface only when the value is taken (Ractor::RemoteError): a Ractor that is never joined hides its failure.
